blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The Friedman test compares three or more related measurements, such as the same patients at several time points. It ranks each subject’s own measurements separately and tests whether some condition tends to get the higher ranks. It is the rank-based counterpart of repeated-measures ANOVA (recall §9.5.5).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
Kruskal-Wallis ranks everybody together. Friedman ranks within each person, so differences between people (one patient always reports more pain than another) drop out, exactly as pairing does in the paired t-test. Only the order of each person’s own scores is used, so an ordinal outcome is fine. With n subjects, k conditions and rank sums R₁ … Rₖ:

Fr = [12 ÷ (nk(k + 1))] × Σ Rⱼ² − 3n(k + 1), approximately χ² with k − 1 df.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Six patients score pain (0–10) before physiotherapy, immediately after, and one month later. Patient 1 scores 7, 4, 3, so the ranks are 3, 2, 1. Across the six patients, “before” gets rank 3 every time.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
1. Rank sums (ties within a patient share ranks): before 18, after 10.5, one month 7.5.
  2. Fr = 12 ÷ (6 × 3 × 4) × (18² + 10.5² + 7.5²) − 3 × 6 × 4 = (1/6) × 490.5 − 72 = 9.75, on 2 df.
  3. The critical value is 5.99, so p < 0.05. A correction for the one tied pair, which software applies automatically, raises Fr to 10.17 (p = 0.006). With only six patients the χ² approximation is rough, and this small example is for arithmetic only.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
pain <- matrix(c(7,4,3,  6,5,4,  8,5,5,  5,3,4,  7,6,3,  6,4,2),
               ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE,
               dimnames = list(paste0("P", 1:6),
                               c("before", "after", "month1")))
t(apply(pain, 1, rank))        # ranks within each patient
friedman.test(pain)
   before after month1
P1      3   2.0    1.0
P2      3   2.0    1.0
P3      3   1.5    1.5
P4      3   1.0    2.0
P5      3   2.0    1.0
P6      3   2.0    1.0

    Friedman rank sum test

data:  pain
Friedman chi-squared = 10.174, df = 2, p-value = 0.006177

The rank table is step 1 (column sums 18, 10.5, 7.5). The statistic is the tie-corrected version of step 2.

points.html: Ranking happens within each subject, never across subjects. That is the structural difference from Kruskal-Wallis.
A significant result says only that the conditions are not all alike. Pairwise follow-up uses Wilcoxon or sign tests on the pairs, with a multiplicity adjustment (recall §9.5.3).

questions.prompt: Match each test to its parametric counterpart: Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, Kruskal-Wallis, Friedman.
questions.answer: Mann-Whitney U ↔︎ independent-samples t-test; Wilcoxon signed-rank ↔︎ paired t-test; Kruskal-Wallis ↔︎ one-way ANOVA; Friedman ↔︎ repeated-measures ANOVA.

questions.prompt: Two groups of 5 are ranked together. Group 1 holds ranks 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7. Compute R₁, U₁ and U₂.
questions.answer: R₁ = 1 + 2 + 4 + 5 + 7 = 19. U₁ = R₁ − n₁(n₁ + 1)/2 = 19 − 15 = 4. U₂ = n₁n₂ − U₁ = 25 − 4 = 21. (Check: group 2 holds ranks 3, 6, 8, 9, 10, sum 36, and 36 − 15 = 21.)

questions.prompt: A Mann-Whitney test is significant, but the two groups have almost identical medians. How can that happen, and how should you report it?
questions.answer: The Mann-Whitney test asks whether values in one group tend to be larger than in the other. It compares medians only if the two distributions have the same shape. If one group is much more spread out or differently skewed, the test can be significant with similar medians (Hart, 2001). Report it as a difference in distribution (“values in group A tend to be higher”), describe both medians and spreads (e.g. IQRs), and do not claim that the medians differ.
